_readme: Thresholds below are CONFIGURABLE reference points used by this prototype's alert engine. Where a value is defined by an official NASA standard, the citation says so explicitly. Where NASA does not publish a specific numeric requirement (e.g. exact vitals cutoffs), the citation says the value is a general clinical / operational reference used for demo purposes, not an official NASA number. Do not present anything in this file as a certified flight requirement.

heart_rate_bpm.source: General clinical resting heart-rate reference range (not NASA-specific). Individual astronaut baselines vary; this prototype also compares against each crew member's own 7-day baseline.

respiration_rate.source: General clinical respiration-rate reference range (not NASA-specific).

spo2_pct.source: General clinical SpO2 reference range (not NASA-specific).

skin_temp_c.source: General clinical body-temperature reference range (not NASA-specific).

sleep.source: NASA schedules 8.5 h of sleep per night in flight, but the largest study of spaceflight sleep found crews average only ~5.96 h (Shuttle) and ~6.09 h (ISS) per night. (Barger LK, et al. 'Prevalence of sleep deficiency and use of hypnotic drugs in astronauts before, during, and after spaceflight.' Lancet Neurology, 2014;13:904-912.) This prototype flags a trailing 3-day average below 7.0 h as ATTENTION and below 6.0 h as CRITICAL, i.e. at/below the historical spaceflight average.

exercise.source: ISS crews are prescribed about 2.5 h/day of aerobic + resistance exercise, 6 days/week, as a countermeasure to cardiovascular and musculoskeletal deconditioning (Ploutz-Snyder L., 'An Evidence-Based Approach to Exercise Prescriptions on ISS,' NASA JSC; Smith SM, et al., J Bone Miner Res, 2012).

wellbeing_1_5.source: Simple 1-5 daily self-assessment scale defined for this prototype (mood, stress, fatigue, motivation, social wellbeing), per the challenge brief. Not a clinical or diagnostic instrument.

musculoskeletal.source: Weight-bearing bone sites lose an estimated 0.4-2.7% BMD per month in microgravity absent effective countermeasures; recovery after return can take a year or more and is not always complete (Sibonga JD, et al.; Lang T, et al.; cited in NASA/TM-2018-219938). Long-duration ISS/Mir crews without adequate resistance exercise have shown >10% loss at some skeletal sites (Shackelford LC, et al.). Adequately varied, high-compliance resistance exercise combined with proper nutrition has been shown to preserve BMD and bone mass in most regions (Smith SM, et al., 2012). This prototype computes a MODELED, NOT MEASURED, cumulative loss estimate from mission duration and each crew member's average resistance-exercise compliance — it is not a substitute for real bone densitometry.

co2_mmhg.source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D [V2 6004] limits the average 1-hour cabin CO2 partial pressure (ppCO2) to no more than 3.0 mmHg, chosen to keep headache incidence below ~1.4%. Historically, ISS has operated in the 1-9 mmHg range with typical operations nearer 4.0 mmHg using CDRA; reported symptoms (headache, fatigue, malaise) increase between 2.8-4.5 mmHg and further above 4.5 mmHg. (OCHMO Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-004, 'Carbon Dioxide.')

o2_pp_mmhg.source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 [V2 6003] defines a 145-155 mmHg O2 partial-pressure normoxia target range for crew exposure. (OCHMO Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-002, 'Environmental Control & Life Support System.')

cabin_pressure_psia.source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 [V2 6006/HS3004] sets a nominal indefinite-exposure total-pressure tolerance band of 7.5-15.0 psia for vehicle operations, with typical shirtsleeve operations nearer 14.7 psia. This prototype uses a narrower comfort/nominal band inside that certified envelope and flags approach toward its edges.

cabin_temp_c.source: NASA-STD-3001 requires the cabin atmosphere be maintained between 18-27 degC (64.4-80.6 degF) during nominal flight operations. (NASA Human Integration Design Handbook / NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2.)

humidity_pct.source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 specifies an allowable relative-humidity range of roughly 25-75%, with 40-60% preferred for comfort. (OCHMO Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-002 / OCHMO-TB-003.)

resources.source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 references an average dietary intake near 3,035 kcal/day per crewmember [V2 7003] and a minimum potable water allowance of 2.5 L/day per crewmember [V2 6109]. Remaining-days thresholds (14-day ATTENTION / 7-day CRITICAL buffer) are an operational planning heuristic defined for this prototype, not an official NASA requirement.
